=== IMM Comments on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777 (Final).pdf ===
Memorandum
TO:      Public Utility Commission of Texas

FROM: Jeff McDonald; Andrew Reimers

DATE:    March 2, 2026

RE:      IMM Commentary on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777


We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the parameters that will be used to assess the
ERCOT system relative to the Reliability Standard. Below we provide some general comments,
followed by comments on questions and aspects highlighted by the PUCT.

A.    General Comments

It is extremely difficult to achieve a 1-in-10 reliability standard in an energy-only market. To
achieve such a standard through shortage pricing alone, the operational VOLL would have to be
large. In other markets, we have previously estimated that VOLL would have to be around
$200,000-$300,000/MWh to achieve a singular 1-in-10 reliability standard. The three-part
reliability standard approved in ERCOT would likely require a VOLL much higher than that.
This is why most other RTOs have a capacity market, which does not appear to be an option in
the ERCOT market. As such, ERCOT and the PUCT will need to consider market design
improvements suitable for Texas in the event the Reliability Standard Assessment indicates the
ERCOT system will not meet the Reliability Standard in a reasonable amount of time.

While the year 2029 may be a reasonable outlook for whether the current market design will
satisfy the Reliability Standard, it is not a sufficient look-out period to evaluate whether potential
market design changes will fill the gap and achieve the Reliability Standard. The time for
formulation, stakeholder consideration, and software design and implementation of a new major
market feature in addition to time for a price signal to incent investment and the gestation period
for new investment likely extend the effective look-out period well beyond 2029. This will be
important if the Reliability Standard Assessment shows a significant projected deficit… Texas’
resource adequacy will hinge on the path to an equilibrium planning reserve margin and not
simply on maintaining that equilibrium once reached.

On modeling both the potential market changes to meet the Reliability Standard and the path to
equilibrium, we note that a model that explicitly includes endogenous capacity expansion will be
necessary. For the Reliability Standard assessment, failure to adequately account for generation
growth will overstate any measured deficiency compared to the Reliability Standard. The Texas
market is designed to produce higher prices and revenue as the system grows tighter (e.g. the

PUBLIC                                                                     © 2025 Potomac Economics
                                            IMM Comments on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777
                                                                                   March 2, 2026



planning reserve decreases). At a point this will induce investment in new generation. If this is
not modeled, the results will falsely show a bias toward greater deficiency as load grows, the
planning reserve margin lessens, and generation additions do not materialize despite market price
signals. Additional market design will be considered to meet the Reliability Standard if it appears
that the current design will not come sufficiently close. In this case, as stated above, the path to
meeting the Reliability Standard and how the alternatives considered provide capacity expansion
along that path will be vital in assessing which market design alternative is best for Texas.

Lastly, there is also an issue regarding which load forecast to use in the Reliability Standard
Assessment. There are several approaches (generally speaking) employed and/or considered
including what is used in the CDR, the Large Load Forecast, the Large Load Interconnection
process (current and proposed), and the Batch process for interconnecting large load. In order to
obtain the most reasonable assessment of whether ERCOT will meet the Reliability Standard it is
important that the most restrictive of these methodologies is used. At a high level, a simultaneous
feasibility approach that considers transmission and resource adequacy constraints should be
applied to achieve a realistic load forecast. Otherwise, load growth will be overstated resulting in
a higher likelihood of greater measured deficiency which could trigger action that is costly and
not needed.

We recommend that:

       1.   When evaluating new market features to achieve the Reliability Standard, use a look-
            ahead period sufficient to allow for design and debate, implementation, and time-to-
            market for new investment.
       2.   Include endogenous growth in any simulation model that is used to evaluate
            alternative market enhancements to meet the Reliability Standard.
       3.   The method used for load growth projections in the Reliability Standard Assessment
            should include simultaneous feasibility, transmission constraints, and resource
            adequacy constraints.

B.    Responses to Commission Questions

1) At the July 25, 2024, open meeting, the Commission approved setting the CONE at
   $140,000/MW-year for planning purposes in the ERCOT region, including the triennial
   reliability assessment. Based on stakeholder feedback, ERCOT has proposed a plan for
   updating this CONE value.
     a. Does CONE need to be updated for the 2026 reliability standard assessment? Why or
        why not?
     b. If the Commission considers an updated CONE value, are the scope and list of tasks
        proposed by Brattle and Sargent & Lundy in ERCOT's January 15, 2026, filing an
        acceptable method to update the calculations? If not, please provide recommended
        modifications to their approach.



PUBLIC                                       2
                                           IMM Comments on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777
                                                                                  March 2, 2026



We recognize that CONE is important in the context of understanding what level of revenue the
ERCOT market needs to produce in order to incent investment in new generation. CONE, and
VOLL, are difficult concepts to measure in a single point estimate due to various factors. We do
support periodic updates to CONE but note that in the context of the ERCOT market the VOLL
is also impactful on market revenue. While CONE is used to trigger a cap of sorts in the spot
market (a la the Peaker Net Margin), the VOLL directly limits price formation. We encourage
the PUCT to provide periodic updates to both figures and to consider the difference between the
“operational” VOLL that is used to limit price formation and the “planning” VOLL that is
applied for out-planning of resource adequacy. A shortage pricing solution to the resource
adequacy problem will require more in-market revenue which is currently limited by both CONE
and the “operational” VOLL which is considerably lower than the “planning” VOLL

2) ERCOT has requested the Commission consider whether the load forecasts used in this study
   should align with the one that will be generated through the 2026 RTP compliance plan
   described in the Commission's rulemaking in Project No. 58480. ERCOT acknowledges that
   an updated load forecast that aligns with that compliance plan could be ready by April or
   May 2026, which would push back the timeline of the reliability assessment by at least a
   month.

       a. Should the Commission approve updating the load forecast used in the 2026
          reliability assessment to align with the compliance plan being considered in Project
          No. 58480, even if it will delay work on the reliability assessment?

Having an updated load forecast is useful, especially as data is constantly evolving. The method
used to produce the load forecast will directly impact the measures result of the Reliability
Standard assessment. Please see our general comments above for more on this.

       b. What other considerations should the Commission make regarding the load forecast
          used for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years?

Please see our general comments above for more on this.

3) ERCOT proposed using the December 2025 Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (CDR) Report
   to create the base portfolio for evaluating the bulk power system in 2026 and 2029. This
   includes resource additions and retirements.

       a. Does the generation portfolio in the December 2025 CDR Report adequately capture
          the resource mix in both 2026 and 2029? If not, what additional assumptions should
          be made about resource additions and retirements?

The CDR generation additions only capture expected additions about two years out. It does not
consider any additions after that. When modeling reserve margin, as the Reliability Standard
assessment will do, it is important to factor in price and investment dynamics. As described
above, as the reserve margin diminishes price and revenue will increase. At some point, this will
incent new investment. This is an important aspect of the ERCOT market and will not be
captured if the CDR generation additions alone are used and extrapolated out to 2029. It is not a

PUBLIC                                      3
                                            IMM Comments on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777
                                                                                   March 2, 2026



simple task to model endogenous investment, however in this type of assessment it is crucial to
account for the investment incentives that will be produced by severely declining reserve
margins. Please see our general comments for more on the importance of accurately modeling
generation additions.

4) Based on information provided by the transmission operators, ERCOT proposed using
   13,988 MW as the magnitude criterion of the reliability standard for the 2026 simulation
   year. For the 2029 simulation year, ERCOT proposes scaling the 2026 magnitude value by
   the ratio of the 75th percentile load forecast for 2029 to the 75th percentile load forecast for
   2026, resulting in a magnitude value of 14,509 MW for the 2029 simulation year.

       a. Should the Commission use these values for the magnitude criterion in the 2026 and
          2029 simulation years? If not, what modifications to these values should be made?

No comment.

5) ERCOT proposed using the EIA' s 2025 Annual Energy Outlook and EIA Form 923 data to
   determine the natural gas and coal prices for the 2026 and 2029 simulation years. This
   results in prices of $2.84/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.47/MMBtu for coal in 2026 and
   $3.16/MMBtu for natural gas and $2.41/MMBtu for coal in 2029.

       a. Are these assumptions for fuel prices for the 2026/2029 simulation years reasonable?
          If not, what alternative sources of information should be considered to determine
          these fuels prices?

       b. Should any sensitivity analyses on these fuel prices be considered?

These values may be fine. In the alternative, more recent futures prices could be substituted
where available.

6) For previous reliability assessments, ERCOT has treated all historical weather years as
   having equal probability. For this assessment, ERCOT proposed weighing recent years more
   heavily.

       a. Should the Commission consider not treating all historical weather years as having
          equal probability? If yes, do you agree with ERCOT's proposed weighting of weather
          years?

All weather years should be treated equally. If all weather years are not treated equally, ERCOT
should provide empirical analysis supporting an alternate weighting. Ideally, this analysis would
look back much further than 44 years and demonstrate that the recent 44 years have a
heterogeneous nature (a) not seen in prior 44 year periods and (b) that reflects an underlying
hypothesis that weather has fundamentally changed in recent years.




PUBLIC                                       4
                                           IMM Comments on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777
                                                                                  March 2, 2026



       b. If you have an alternative weighting methodology, please provide additional details
          on your proposal. Please include justification for why your approach is better than
          what ERCOT has proposed.

7) ERCOT proposed using the multi-area reliability and economic dispatch modeling capability
   in SERVM to assess resource adequacy on a zonal basis that would account for transmission
   constraints between defined transmission zones. ERCOT states that any results from this
   analysis would be informational and not used to determine compliance with the reliability
   standard.

       a. Should the Commission approve an assessment of reliability metrics at the zonal
          level, understanding that these results would be purely informational and not used to
          determine compliance with the reliability standard?

This would provide additional information that may be useful in how the ERCOT system is
considered (as a whole or as zones). This, in fact, may help inform ERCOT and stakeholders of a
need to update existing load zones which the IMM has previously recommended.

       b. If so, do you have any proposed modifications to the approach ERCOT has
          recommended?

8) ERCOT proposed modifying how the model accounts for the effectiveness of the
   Commission's weatherization rule 16 TAC § 25.55. Previously, it was estimated to reduce
   weather-related outages by 85%, however under ERCOT's proposed approach, the rule' s
   effectiveness would decline during extreme temperatures

       a. Do you agree with ERCOT's recommendation to deviate from the 85% effectiveness
          for the weatherization rule?

The weatherization rule was put forth to address availability under extreme conditions. Using an
85% effectiveness factor already accounts for some “slippage” which is to be expected. If an
alternate effectiveness schedule is to be used there should be empirical evidence provided to
support the proposed schedule. Without that, no alternate effectiveness schedule should be used.

9) ERCOT has proposed assumptions for the outages:

       a. Are the assumptions for generation and ESR outage modeling reasonable? If not,
          what modifications do you propose?

       b. How should ERCOT treat planned transmission outages in the model?

No comment on a or b.

10) Please provide comments and recommendations on any of the model input assumptions that
    Staff has not specifically flagged in previous questions.



PUBLIC                                      5
          IMM Comments on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777
                                                 March 2, 2026




PUBLIC     6
                                          IMM Comments on Reliability Standard Assessment 58777
                                                                                 March 2, 2026



C.   Executive Summary – Potomac Economics – Independent Market Monitor



A general characterization of our responses to PUCT questions is that empirical analysis should
be the motivator of many of the decisions made regarding modeling parameters. This type of
analysis can have profound implications regarding market policy going forward. As such, the
parameters and the model itself must be calibrated to provide the most accurate projections of
potential planning reserve margin.

In addition to responses to PUCT questions, we provide general comments on the approach that
culminate in the following recommendations:

     1.    When evaluating new market features to achieve the Reliability Standard, use a look-
           ahead period sufficient to allow for design and debate, implementation, and time-to-
           market for new investment.
     2.    Include endogenous growth in any simulation model that is used to evaluate
           alternative market enhancements to meet the Reliability Standard.
     3.    The method used for load growth projections in the Reliability Standard Assessment
           should include simultaneous feasibility, transmission constraints, and resource
           adequacy constraints.
